title: A month of moon days
hook: keeping the uposatha on each quarter moon for a month

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the list with the sixth perfection: wisdom, seeing things as they are, in every act. Did you catch one ordinary moment and see that it was changing? Day one thousand four hundred five.

Before dawn on a full moon morning in a Theravada country, people dressed in white walk to the monastery. Some carry food for the monks. At the hall they kneel, and a monk leads them through the precepts, line by line in Pali, and they repeat after him. Then they stay. They will not eat after midday. They will sit, listen to a talk, chant, maybe sleep on a mat on the floor. Tomorrow they go back to ordinary life. A week or so later, when the moon is half, some of them will come back. Today, not one moon day, but a whole month of them.
screen: `WHITE CLOTHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `A DAY AND A NIGHT OF PRECEPTS.` → `THEN, WHEN THE MOON IS HALF, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The day is called uposatha, an observance day, and it follows the moon: the new moon, the full moon, and the half-moons in between. In the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha describes how a lay follower keeps it. For one day and one night, they take on eight precepts instead of the usual five. No killing, no stealing. Not just no sexual misconduct, but no sex at all for the day. No false speech, no intoxicants. And three more: no food after midday, no dancing, music, shows, perfume or jewelry, and no high, luxurious bed. Each one, the text says, is kept the way the arahants, the fully awakened, keep it all their lives. The lay person says, in effect: for this day and this night, I'll live as they do. That's the heart of it. A moon day is a borrowed day. You try on, for a single turn of the clock, the life of someone fully free. Then you give it back. And here is why a month matters. One moon day can be a nice experience. Four in a row, spaced by the moon, start to become a rhythm. Each time, the precepts feel a little more familiar, the hungry evening a little less strange, the quiet a little less loud. The moon does the remembering for you. You don't have to decide when to practice. You just look up. Across a month, the moon days turn from an event into a calendar, and the calendar quietly turns into a life.
screen: `UPOSATHA FOLLOWS THE MOON.` · `EIGHT PRECEPTS FOR A DAY AND A NIGHT.` · `LIVING AS THE ARAHANTS DO.` · then, large: `THE MOON DOES THE REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, get your phone or a calendar ready for a moment, then set it down and sit first. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind the shape of the moon tonight. You may not know it, and that's fine. Then, after the bell, look up the coming new moon, full moon and the two half-moons, and mark them. Next to each, write one small thing you might keep that day: no food after midday, no music, a quiet evening, or simply a few minutes of sitting. Nothing has to be decided now except the dates. The bell holds the time.
A month of moon days. Uposatha, the observance day, kept on the new, full and half moons, borrowing for a day and a night the life of the awakened. Today's word.
screen: `A MONTH OF MOON DAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a month of moon days. Tonight, if the sky is clear, step outside and find the moon. Notice its shape, and how many days until it changes. Day one thousand four hundred five.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries such as Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, devout lay Buddhists keep uposatha days on the new, full and half moons, often wearing white, going to the monastery and taking the eight precepts for a day and a night.

original.note: Pali uposatha: the observance day, kept on the new, full and half moons.

trapdoor: what you thought: a moon day is a festival once in a while.
what it means: uposatha, a day and a night of eight precepts, kept with every phase of the moon.
what a scholar hears: the Numerical Discourses' account of the eight-factored uposatha, kept 'as the arahants do', the lay person borrowing the awakened life for a day.

notes: AN 8.41 paraphrased: the eight factors and the refrain that the arahants abstain all their lives, 'today I too for this night and day'. Confirm the list wording (dancing, singing, music, shows, garlands, scents, adornment; high and luxurious beds).
'Eight precepts instead of the usual five' is the cited text's count plus the five precepts; confirm.
Uposatha on new, full and half moons: Sutta Nipata 2.14 mentions the fourteenth, fifteenth and eighth of the fortnight; kept as 'new, full and half moons' without numbers. Confirm.
Hook scene (white clothes, Pali precepts repeated after a monk, food for monks, floor mats) is illustrative of Theravada practice; 'a week or so later' is the half-moon interval. Confirm.
Pronunciation oo-POH-sa-ta (th in Pali is an aspirated t); confirm.
